The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. 417, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act-Mr. Prudham-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Application of act to 1955, 1956, 1957 and 1958.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: In speaking on second reading last evening, I asked the government, through either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, to make some statement concerning government policy, the kind of policy that might, we hope, lead to a solution of the problems of the gold mining industry rather than simply depending upon stop-gap emergency palliatives of the kind embodied in the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. May I ask the ministers if they will now make a statement of government policy in that regard? That statement should embrace government policy in regard to the price of gold so far as that is determined by the international monetary fund; second, their efforts to persuade the government of the United States .to increase the price at which it is prepared to buy newly mined Canadian gold and, third, the policy of the Canadian government in purchasing newly mined gold for the Canadian government's own reserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that the question the hon. member has brought up with regard to the government's policy of holding gold reserves could much better

be directed to the Minister of Finance when his estimates are before the house. So far as the efforts of the government to persuade the United States to increase the price of gold are concerned, I am sure that everything possible has been done in that regard. The fact that the United States is willing to buy all the gold offered at $35 per ounce gives a stability to the gold mining industry that does not exist in any other section of the mining industry or any other industry that I know of.
Hon. members have urged that the United States be requested to abandon that policy and to free the market for gold. As yet I have never heard anyone in the gold mining industry suggest that would be a good thing. At the present time the so-called free market for gold is below the fixed price of $35 per ounce. The high prices that have been quoted as having been obtained on the free market in years past have, I think, been related to conditions of panic that existed in various parts of the world and in no sense could be considered a stable market. The present quotation of between $34 and $35 an ounce in Switzerland would of course be decreased by the cost of transportation of gold to that country and the various service charges involved.
I believe that at the present time the fixed price of gold is really a stabilizing influence in the industry. We all admit it would be much better for the industry if the price were raised, but the raising of the price of gold would simply mean that the United States would be willing to give more United States goods and services for an ounce of gold.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: Or dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: Or dollars. I contend that is a decision that rests with the United States. All producing countries would favour an increase in the price of gold, but in the final analysis it is a decision that the United States will have to make.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
I am not at all unmindful of what the minister has called the stabilizing effect of the assured market for gold production in the United States. Undoubtedly it has been a supporting and guaranteeing factor of considerable importance to the gold mining industry that there has always been that assured market at the price of $35 U.S. per ounce. Whatever has been said in times past about freeing the market has never been put forward by anyone, as far as I am aware, with any thought of losing the benefit of the assured market and assured price in the United States.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I may do so, I should like to answer this question instead of my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I am not aware of any action that has been taken by this government with respect to asking the United States government to increase the price of gold. The answer which was last made on this subject in the house was made by my predecessor about three years ago now. At that time he made it quite clear that he realized it would be in the interests of the gold mining industry and the gold producers of Canada that there should be a higher price for gold. But he also made it clear that that was a matter which rested solely in the hands of the United States government which purchased the gold and that he did not feel that we should interfere in what he at that time termed a domestic matter in the United States. That answer was made by him in the course of a certain amount of questioning by my friend the hon. member for Eglinton, and I think it was his policy until he left office. Certainly it has been mine since I entered into the office on July 1, 1954.

It would be a matter of the administration recommending to congress and congress taking the appropriate action to increase the gold content of the dollar. The statement that this is a matter of purely United States domestic concern completely ignores the fact that this is a matter of very lively concern to the Canadian economy. I do not at all follow the remarks of the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman, when he says that the price the United States is prepared to pay for gold is established by congress, and for that reason the Canadian government should not make representations to the United States administration in that regard. Surely, that is a very far-fetched kind of theory, because many of the fields in which representations are being made, as we understand it, on the part of the Canadian government to the United States administration at Washington are fields in which action is required or action has been taken by the United States congress. Of course, action on the part of congress would be required to change the price that the United States is prepared to pay for gold, but surely that is no reason why representations ought not to be made by the Canadian government to the United States administration, if it is in the interests of this country to seek an increase in the price the United States government is prepared to pay for newly mined Canadian gold. It is perfectly obvious, Mr. Chairman, there is no likelihood of the administration at Washington making any recommendation to congress in this regard if the Canadian government is not prepared to support the interests of Canada and of the Canadian gold mining industry by making representations to the United States administration at Washington to the same effect.
I think it has been made quite clear here today that one minister considers Canada should seek on the part of the United States administration an increase in the price they are prepared to pay for newly mined Canadian gold. It is perfectly evident at the same time that the Minister of Finance, and I take

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act it the rest of the government, concurs in a policy of remaining silent and ignoring this problem and doing nothing to lay the interests of Canada before the United States administration at Washington with suitable representations in that regard. If that is the lackadaisical kind of attitude the Canadian government is going to take we shall be obliged to go on with the kind of measure now before us-hand-to-mouth, stop-gap, emergency, palliative measures-and ignore the essence of the problem and the need for facing up to it and seeking a solution.
If the Canadian government does not see fit to make any kind of representations in this matter to the United States administration at Washington, our nearest neighbour, I suppose there is not much use expecting this government to make any representations in the interests of the Canadian economy at meetings of the board of governors of the international monetary fund.
We do know that the South African government is not labouring under any such apathy or inhibitions. The South African government, as one of the great gold producing countries of the world, has not hesitated to lay its case before the international monetary fund and to request action on the part of that fund to increase the price of newly mined gold; but the Canadian government apparently is content to remain apathetic, lackadaisical and silent. Well, Mr. Chairman, that policy is just not good enough. It is that policy evidently that is making it necessary to continue measures of the kind we have before us. Of course, the gold mining industry should not be permitted to suffer further in the face of the apathy and indifference of this government. We shall have to have measures of this kind as long as the government is going to shirk its duty and ignore its responsibility; but believe me, Mr. Chairman, this government is going to have to face the strongest kind of criticism of which the opposition is capable if the government is going to go on ignoring the problem and the need of finding a solution.

There is just one minister, and I give him credit for it, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, who had the courage and the realistic appreciation of the plight of the Canadian gold producers, and with that the plight of their employees and the communities dependent upon those mines, to lay this problem even briefly before President Eisenhower when he was here and to ask the president what the United States administration might be prepared to do.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up more time of the committee than is necessary and I shall be brief in my remarks. However, I cannot allow this legislation to pass without saying a word on behalf of the gold miners, the ordinary working men, the businessmen and the small property owners of my constituency. The people of northwestern Quebec were not only pleased when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was enacted in 1948 and extended thereafter; they were greatly relieved because one of the principal industries of the district was able to continue its operations. They have been grateful to the government. Although they were convinced

that some form of assistance was forthcoming, they appreciate the fact that this legislation is passed at this time.
From what has been said during the course of this debate it is evident that hon. members on all sides of the house are satisfied that this legislation should be extended for another period of two years. The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is evidence of the recognition by the government of the importance of the gold mining industry in the national economy. The welfare of the gold mining industry has always been regarded by the government and by parliament as of great importance. For this I wish to express my thanks for the fact that the government has come forward at this time with this legislation which is encouraging to industry and to residents of gold mining communities. We are all grateful for that.
When this legislation was enacted in 1948, and when it was extended and amended from time to time, there was little or no opposition. For this the residents of the gold mining communities are certainly grateful to all hon. members on all sides of this house. However, for the benefit and information of those who may have some doubt as to the wisdom of this legislation, I wish to repeat what I have said on numerous occasions when I have had the privilege of speaking on this matter.
It is true that there was no definite opposition to the measure, but from time to time hon. members have expressed the opinion that there have been some abuses in connection with this form of assistance and that it did not benefit the miners and communities dependent upon the industry as it should have done.
In 1947 the average annual wage of a miner working in a Canadian gold mine was $2,277; the corresponding figure for 1950 was $2,763, an increase of 21-3 per cent over 1947. In 1954 the average wage of a miner working in a Canadian gold mine was $3,400, an increase of 49 per cent over 1947. For the period for which figures are available from the dominion bureau of statistics, that is from 1948 to 1954 inclusive, we find that the total increase in wages and salaries paid by the gold producers was equivalent to more than 85 per cent of the total assistance paid by the Canadian government.
During that same period the gold mining industry paid over $40 million in federal, provincial and municipal taxes, which item alone represents 50 per cent of the total assistance received. During the same period the total amount of wages and salaries paid by the gold mining industry amounted to $443 million. The aggregate cost of supplies,
13, 1956	4991
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act plant and equipment, buildings and machinery in the same period amounted to $383 million. These figures are impressive and it is important to take them into consideration. While wages, supplies and freight are the principal items of cost in operating a mine, they are by no means the only factors which contribute to an increase in the cost of operation. In addition, account must be taken of improved health and welfare services, increased rates of workmen's compensation and many other items which total some quite substantial amounts.
We must be reminded that the gold mining industry is the only industry which has to absorb these increases in the cost of operation without being able to pass on to the consumer any portion of the increased costs. In order to give a striking example to hon. members of this house and to establish the extent to which operating expenses have increased in the gold mining industry during the last 15 years I should like to cite some figures taken from the annual report of an important gold mine in my own home town of Malartic.
During the year 1940 the gross revenue of this mine was $3,424,000, substantially the same as for 1955 when it amounted to $3,473,000. However, in 1940 the operating costs were $1,319,000 with a net profit of $1,568,000. In 1955, notwithstanding more efficient mechanical equipment and other economies, the costs soared to $2,527,000 while the net profit shrank to $261,000.
The price of gold has been kept down to the 1934 basis of $35 U. S. per ounce while the cost of production has gone away up. In view of this it must be realized that the industry has no alternative but to accept government assistance even if this assistance falls short of compensating for the rise in production costs.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say something regarding the dividends which are being paid out from time to time by Canadian gold mines. The remark was made the other day that in one year the dividends paid out by Canadian gold mines amounted to $18 million and that these gold mining companies received $16 million in subsidies from the government. I did not verify the amount of $18 million paid out in dividends by the Canadian gold mines during 1954, but I accept this figure. However, I wish to say this, in order to put the record straight. The gold mines that did not alter their dividend rates and those which are paying the bulk of this $18 million in dividends are those which are not in the receipt of assistance.
Whatever dividends are being paid these days by most of the gold mines are taken
4992	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act from surplus earned from other sources than their actual operations. Others are squeezing their dividends from accumulated surplus earned during the good years before the second world war. Many other gold mines are not paying any dividends at all. How long they will be able to continue to do that, we do not know. For how long they will be able to ask their shareholders to be patient, we do not know either. They certainly cannot tell their shareholders that this is a new way of operating a business.
From 1948 to 1954 inclusive, out of 27 Quebec gold mines which received assistance from the government, 15 never paid any dividends. Five others paid less than $500,000 each during those seven years. The six other remaining gold mines paid dividends on a reduced rate, and it is important to note that during that same period those six gold mines paid over $75,000 in increased wages alone, over and above what they received in assistance from the government.
The shareholders in the Canadian gold mining industry number many thousands and the great majority of them are small shareholders. We must keep that in mind. I will go so far as to say that the government, both in its role of tax collector and in its role of representative of the broader interests of all Canadians, has the responsibility to hang on to the gold mining industry, and hanging on to the gold mining industry means helping the shareholders, the employees, the small property owners, the farmers and the business people dependent on gold mining.
I also wish to remind the members of this house that the gold mining industry, important as it is, is only one branch of the metal mining industry of this country. This mining industry gives employment to some 130,000 men, who in turn are the supporters of more than 500,000 people. So, in trying to establish some comparison between the assistance allocated to the gold mines and that which is granted to other key industries, it would be only fair to keep those figures in mind.
An advance in the price of gold, I will admit, is the only permanent solution to the problem of the Canadian gold mines; but, as our country is not the largest producer or the largest seller of the precious metal, we cannot dictate a price and much less influence buyers by refusing to sell. We are faced with this problem, that the price of gold can be raised only by joint international action in which the initiative rests with our neighbours to the south, the United States of America.
The Canadian gold mining industry is passing through very difficult years, and the only final solution lies in a realistic valuation for gold in terms of the inflated United States


dollar. The argument that this would result in further inflation and would help the communist nations more than those of the free world is only wishful thinking.
Meanwhile we are all aware that the production and sale of gold are of great importance to the Canadian economy. As it is, and until there is an increase in the price of gold, we must agree that the government will have to continue its assistance to the gold mines of our country.

I think it is important -as I perhaps said the last time this matter was up for consideration-that this question of the standard of living and the working conditions that are going to apply under the circumstances where the public funds are being paid out should be of great concern to the members of this house. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys earlier made reference to some figures, and mentioned the number of immigrants who had been brought into the country to work in mines. However, I think it might perhaps be fair to say that the admittedly substandard or-and I think this was the word used by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys yesterday-lower wage rates and the admittedly somewhat poorer working conditions that apply in the gold mining industry when contrasted with those in the base metal mines have probably resulted in a large proportion of those immigrants who have come to work in mines ending up in the gold mining camps. This would be generally true in the mining industry as a whole.
I know-and I mention this because it verifies in part the claims that were made by the hon. member for Kootenay West last night-that in one of the gold mining camps in central British Columbia which I visited last summer-actually it was part of a holiday trip on the way home from the end of the session-that that particular matter was drawn to my attention in conversations I had while I was there. By way of explanation, I might say that this was in a gold mining camp in which I had lived for eight or nine years, and that I was talking to people whom I had known since 1933, and who had been continuously since that time-and probably prior to that time in some cases

engaged in one manner or another in the gold mining

industry. That was the comment I heard in that particular camp from a good many quarters, from people who were intimately familiar with all that had gone on in the period that had elapsed since I had left there. That comment was in effect that the mining operation was being flooded by recent immigrants to this country.
I think perhaps it is understandable that the experienced miners of British Columbia who have been in this country over a longer period of years may have gravitated to other mining camps engaged in other phases of the mining industry where wages and conditions may be somewhat better. I think it is an unfortunate situation-and one that should give us pause-to realize that there is a good deal of truth in what the hon. member for Kootenay West was suggesting last night, namely that these people who come as strangers to our land all too often seem to end up in the least desirable situations and occupations that are to be offered in this country. Some might argue that there is perhaps a certain rude justice in that situation and that they should be obliged to do a bit of the dirty work before they graduate into the more lucrative and desirable occupations. Nevertheless there is a tendency-and I have seen too many concrete examples of it here and there; and in this reference I may say I am not referring particularly to the gold mining industry-to exploit these people coming as newly landed immigrants to our shores.
I think it is certainly right that the hon. member for Kootenay West should have raised this particular question while we were considering a bill to extend the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I think we all recognize that a great deal of what was said a short time ago about the situation of the gold mining industry, in the analysis that was given to us, is perfectly true. Anyone who has been associated with the industry in any way or who lived in a gold mining area back in the days of the early 30's recognizes the basic economics of the situation that exists today in relation to the fixed price of gold. But nevertheless, every time this question comes up, as far as I am concerned I feel that every emphasis should be given to the fact that, if we are going to allow this money to be spent from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada for the assistance of this industry, our primary concern should be a humanitarian one.
The place of gold in our economy is a subject that has already been discussed and I would not like to argue with some of the things that have been said both by hon. members from the government side of the house

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act production nor have we lost too much in population. We are not as well off as we were prior to 1948, but by and large the town of Timmins is in good shape and some of the mines are in pretty fair shape, too.
I want to say at this time that the exten-tion of this gold mining assistance act is welcome news to the mines in my community and to the people as a whole. Gold, as some of you know, was third in 1955 amongst the metals mined in the province of Ontario. The Porcupine mines shared in that to the extent of about 45 per cent of Ontario's whole production. You can see from that that gold mining is rather the major and basic industry in Timmins.
Yesterday or the day before there were figures put on the record, and I am not going to get into a controversy with anybody about figures. If I happen to quote figures and they happen to be out a little bit, that is to be understood. In his very fine presentation on behalf of the gold mines I noticed that the minister made a reference to four people being employed on the surface for every one employed underground in the mine. This reference appears on page 4916 of Hansard for June 11, 1956. I think what the minister had in mind was the local vicinity. I am asking that question because I think I have read somewhere, although I could not find it this morning, that for every man employed underground in a gold mine to take out a ton of ore, in the neighbourhood of nine people were supported in other industries and services on the surface. I am not trying to correct the minister in any way whatever, and I may need to be corrected on my own figures.
I noticed in yesterday's Hansard that the hon. member for Spadina spoke for a few minutes about the minting of gold coins. This question was brought up in the house two or three years ago and at that particular time I supported the minting of gold coins. I advocated that we should try it. I notice that you can now carry gold coins with you. In fact, I happened to see the first one in quite a few years the day before yesterday.
I believe it was the hon. member for Kootenay West who referred to immigrants who were brought in to work in the mines. I believe this question was well answered by the Minister of Labour. I have been asked several times why this was allowed, and why the department brought in these immigrants, and I did not know the answers. I understand the policy better now. So far as Mr. Ramsay is concerned, I have known him personally for over 40 years, and they could not have picked a better man to go over to select
(Mr. Eyre.]

help for the mining industry. It was also my understanding that this help was for the mining industry as a whole. I do not agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that the immigrants live in bunkhouses and rooming houses. It has been my observation over the past few years that the men who have come into Porcupine from other countries to work in the mines, a few from England, Scotland, not so many from Ireland, and from Germany or Italy, have all made fine citizens and have bought homes. I think probably the hon. member had in mind the single men who come to that area. It is my understanding that they are bringing married men and their families as well.

speechtext: I was informed that they were largely single men.

speechtext: You spoke of that, but you did not speak about the married men.

I noticed that, according to the newspapers, a fellow in England wanted to come to Canada to work in the gold mines. He was talking to Mr. Ramsay and said he wanted to come. The next day he said, "I cannot go; my wife will not let me. What am I going to do?" Mr. Ramsay said, "You had better take your wife's advice and stay at home." I understand they are bringing married men over here.
Mention was made of the salaries. As I said before, I am going to deal with one mine and I am not going to put the name of the mine on the record. I did not get these figures from the mine but I got them from a source connected with the mining industry. These figures refer to one of our larger mines but they apply to most of the mines in my constituency. In the year 1947 the payroll was over $3 million. In 1954 the payroll was close to $4-5 million, and the average number of employees during all these years runs about the same. In fact, they have 105 more employees now than they had in 1947. Basing it on those figures for 1947 and 1954, I would say that in my opinion every man received a fairly good increase in wages. The figures refer to some members of the staff but do not include management. I am not going into the wage question and try to say what the wage should be.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: What rate per hour are they getting now?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
I cannot put that figure on the record at the moment because I do not happen to have it with me. If you base your calculation on 1,100 men and take a payroll of

$3J million and then take 1,100 men with a payroll of $4-5 million, you will be close. That is just about the way it runs all the way through.
I noticed also that according to yesterday's Hansard the hon. member for St. Paul's spoke. I must say that the hon. member for St. Paul's is quite qualified to speak about gold mines. I know of several with which he is connected in my constituency. The hon. member has dealt with the international monetary fund, and so on. I have no intention of getting involved in a debate on that subject but I will say, sir, that the hon. member for St. Paul's put some fine figures on the record which are general and apply in large part to the mines in my constituency.
The hon. member spoke about the average age of the miners. Having been connected with mining directly and indirectly for a number of years I have built up a substantial library on mining, especially gold mining. I have in my hand some figures covering the pre-war period and up to the end of 1954 as they apply to some of the mines in Porcupine. The average age prior to the war was 35-16 years. The average age in 1954 was 39-09 years. There may be something in what the hon. member for Kootenay West said, because I notice the highest average age in any one mine in 1954 was 41-2 years and the lowest average was 34 years. This, of course, refers to Porcupine only.
I have some further figures which can be verified. Porcupine, including all mines, employed 7,300 men in 1951. At the end of 1954 they employed 6,315 men. There has been a decrease as far as the number of employees is concerned in my constituency.
I must say the new formula that was put in last year is in my opinion the best formula we have had throughout the life of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I would like to see more money available, but be that as it may, I hope the day will come before the act expires when we will not have to ask for any assistance for the gold mines.
Hindsight is so much easier than foresight, but if there had been a formula of this type in operation at the beginning it would have done away with a lot of our troubles. When I refer to our troubles I refer more or less to the controversy concerning wages and things of that nature. There were mines that were receiving a large amount of subsidy, and when you saw headlines in the papers that a mine had paid out two or three million dollars in dividends and received $1 million in subsidy, the reaction right off the bat was that the government was paying 50 per cent of the dividends and that is not a true picture at all.

With reference to the nine men or nine families that were supported by the man in the mine-that may include him also-I would like to leave a thought with you concerning what this means to other communities outside the immediate mining community. If we take 50 per cent of the number of people who are living off the production of a mine as representing those who do not live in the community, in my opinion it affects the prosperity of a great many other communities.
I hold in my hand figures concerning a particular mine. In 1951 this mine purchased $2,422,340 worth of supplies from outside the immediate community. I wish to put on the record the number of communities that benefited from those purchases. In the neighbourhood of 50 communities in Ontario, 14 in Quebec, and St. Boniface, Winnipeg, Port Alberni and Vancouver benefited. You can readily see, therefore, how the purchases of mining communities affect communities outside the mining area. In the good old days- and I mean when the price of gold was high and things were going along pretty well-one mine up there purchased outside supplies to the total value of $5,818,000.50. That is a lot of money to distribute in various communities located outside the mining area, and I notice that the figures for an 8-year period are about the same.
With reference to dividends, I do not know what some people consider a proper dividend to receive on money invested. I guess it is human nature to want to receive all that one can. I have here figures for the year 1951 concerning some mines in my constituency and I notice the yield has been greatly reduced since 1951. I shall not give the name of the mine, but the highest yield on the investment was 7-05 per cent. I find the lowest yield on the investment was 1 [DOT] 80 per cent. This particular mine employs a considerable number of men and at the moment I do not think it would pay any dividend, although of course I do not know.
When the new formula came in I thought it would probably adversely affect the cost of production of mines in my constituency, but I find that it has helped them. I would like to go into that matter for just a moment if I may be allowed the time, Mr. Chairman, and if the hon. members are willing to bear with me; but before I do so let me say a word concerning the number of ounces produced.
The figures I have are not right to the ounce. My constituency produced 110,114 ounces of gold in 1953, a decrease of roughly 17,000 ounces from 1948. In 1955 we produced nearly 84,485 ounces of gold, which was a decrease of approximately 8,796 ounces during the
4998	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act years in which the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been in effect. If you consider the figures for 1948 and 1953 it will be seen that the difference in production is not too great. Taking the 11 producing mines in my constituency-there was one I did not consider because there has been an amalgamation in the last two or three years and I could not separate it-four mines show an increase in production since 1948 while six show a decrease. The increase amounted to over 50,000 ounces while the decrease totalled 71,000 ounces, which left a net difference of approximately 20,000 ounces.
These mines are doing a fine job in trying to keep their costs down. Every man employed in the mines is trying to find ways and means of keeping costs down and inventing ways to do things more cheaply.
For just a moment I should like to deal with the question of secondary industries in northern Ontario as a whole and in my own constituency in particular. This matter has been referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the hon. member for Timiskaming and others, and it has been said that the government should do something to assist in the establishment of secondary industries. I should like to put on the record the fact that two years ago a survey was made in my constituency by most capable men under the direction of the Minister of Defence Production. A report was submitted, and I have hopes that something will be done in the near future.
In addition others have been looking into the possibilities of establishing secondary industries which would be beneficial to Canada as a whole. An association has been formed in northern Ontario to cover the area down to Sault St. Marie and Sudbury. The office is in North Bay and operations are carried on under the direction of the provincial government, which is paying $10,000 a year toward the cost of keeping up that office and employing an administrator, an investigator and so on.
The town of Timmins has an aggressive industrial commission which works in conjunction with the Porcupine chamber of commerce. In the past few months the town of Timmins employed a firm of experts in Montreal to come in and make a survey, working in conjunction with the local industrial commission, the commission set up in North Bay and the dominion government. I have hopes that something will be accomplished in the Porcupine area. If that should come about it would be of assistance also to the hon. member for Timiskaming. We have a few secondary industries, but they are small and are related more to the local scene.


Reference has been made to subsidies and assistance for the gold mines. I appreciate that, and I appreciate also how much it appears to be costing the taxpayers. However, actually I do not think it is costing the taxpayers anything and I shall try to prove my point. The figures I am going to give do not come from the Department of National Revenue or any department of government. In the last couple of years alone over 6,000 miners working in the mines in my constituency have paid nearly $2 million in income tax. I do not know what the other local people would have paid in the same period, but it would be a considerable sum. Then when we consider the industries which are supported by the gold mines we would find that the income tax there would be substantial. The amount received under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in my area in 1953 was a little over $3 million; in 1952 it was around $2 million, and in the years prior to that it was over $3 million.

Mr. Chairman, now that we have heard from the hon. member for Timmins there would seem to be support for the proposition we made to the minister that he should consider amending this bill and restoring the rates which were in effect a year ago. We heard from the hon. member for Ville-neuve, who knows a good deal about this industry, having had long experience as a surveyor, and I believe he agrees with us when we say that while changes in the formula might have to be made from time to time, the substantial reduction which took place last year, amounting to 44 per cent, should be eliminated. On the forecast of next year's payments it will be a reduction of 50 per cent in the course of two years. However, that appears to be the government's fixed intention.
In tribute to the gold mines I wish to put on record one or two facts from the report of the Ontario committee on gold mining, which was referred to last night. That is the committee under the chairmanship of Professor Knox which reported last year to the Ontario government. It collects much useful and up to date information about gold mining in Ontario.
One figure in which I think the committee will be interested is the increase in wages paid by gold mines. The average wage over and above the payment of this assistance has

increased 50 per cent, from about $2,200 to $3,200 a year. For the 10,600 gold miners in Ontario that is something like a $10 million increase in annual wages over the period during which this assistance has been paid, so one can see that the increase in wages paid in Ontario alone is more than the entire subsidy in all Canada in the same period. The entire subsidy is estimated to be $9,300,000. The increase in wages is something like $10,600,000 over the wages paid when the subsidy first came into force. This indicates that the gold mining industry is helping itself as well as receiving this emergency assistance which it needs from the government.
There is a very interesting table, too, on the composition of the men in the different gold mining camps of Ontario, and I commend it to those who have spoken about the age groups. It is an interesting fact that of the 10,988 gold miners who are tabulated and classified according to age at page 84 of this report 2-2 per cent were over 65 years of age, which I think bears out what has been said, that the mechanization of the mines makes it possible for men to carry on after their years of greatest physical vigour. Some 3-5 per cent were between the ages of 60 and 64. I understand that in the civil service a man is considered ineligible after 65, and in some places after 60, but here we have 3-5 per cent of the gold miners in Ontario between the ages of 60 and 65. The table is there for those who wish to see it, and I shall not take the time of the committee to read it. As I say, 64 per cent of the miners were under 44 years of age, but the fact that they are distributed over the entire working period indicates the stability of these communities and the social value of this measure, which will help to save these solid communities where men work throughout their entire working days.
Now I wish to ask one question in concluding my remarks on this section. The minister indicated that five gold mines closed during the past year when the reduced rates of assistance were in force. I should like to have the names of the five mines which found it necessary to close their operations.

speechtext: There was one other matter touched on last night on which nothing has been said yet. The Minister of Finance is not here, although he was here at the opening of the committee sitting this afternoon. There was a matter raised last night in regard to government purchases of gold for various reserve funds that the government maintains, whether in the Bank of Canada or in the exchange funds. Can we have some statement of government policy in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
I believe the government reserves of gold are somewhere about $1 billion. My hon. friend from St. Paul's mentioned the fact that last year I suggested that he was willing to gamble the taxpayers' money. I think it is a matter of exercising good judgment as to how large a reserve the government should hold. If the United States were to take the advice of the hon. member for Spadina, abandon the fixed price for gold and throw the world on the free market again, I am a little doubtful whether it would be considered good business for the government to have as large a hoard as we have right now. On the other hand, if the United States government were to accept the advice of the hon. member for Eglinton and raise the price of gold the government
5000	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act would stand to profit. I think it is just a matter of exercising prudent judgment as to the level at which the government reserves of gold should be maintained. If the fixed price for gold should be abandoned by the United States and the price went down, I am sure my hon. friend would criticize the government for having such a large stock on hand and losing money. On the other hand, if they should raise the price I think he would say we should have had a larger hoard.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
I am a little surprised at the minister's remarks. It does not sound to me as though he entertains much confidence in the future of gold. If he does not entertain much confidence in the future of gold, I think it is going to be a factor in qualifying the outlook for the gold mining industry in this country. I had hoped from what the minister said in his remarks yesterday that he did have a sense of confidence in the future of gold. It is an important industry in this country. If there is no future for gold, there is no future for the gold mining industry in this country.
It seems to me, as I endeavoured to say last night, that the Canadian government could do something quite useful for the outlook for this important industry by showing its confidence in the future of the commodity they are producing. Nobody is proposing any vast increase in the holdings. However, as I indicated last night, while there has been a slight increase in the government's holdings of gold in each of the last four years my information is that in 1956, that portion of it which has elapsed thus far, the government's total gold holding has decreased. That is not a very good advertisement. That does not suggest that the government has confidence in the future of this important Canadian commodity.
I think the minister's last remarks this afternoon are disappointing. Has the minister nothing to say as Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to indicate his confidence in the future of this Canadian commodity, a commodity that is still being sought by every country in the world and which is a factor in the fiscal and trading policies of every country in the world, whatever its system of government, and that includes the totalitarian governments as well? Is the Canadian parliament now to be told that the government is lacking in faith in the future of gold and is timid about making purchases of gold for holding in reserves that the government keeps anyway? After all, it is only a question whether the government holds gold or United States dollars in that fund.


The minister conjures up the possibility of the United States government withdrawing from its policy of purchasing-

I think what the hon. member for Spadina recommended was that more leeway should be given to the Canadian mines to market their product, whether in the free market or in the United States. After all, some of us on this side had to press the government hard before the government embarked several years ago on the policy of permitting sales of gold in the free market, and we had to complain afterwards that the terms upon which the government was permitting those sales in the free market were very rigid. So rigid, in fact, and so stiff were the terms that they really nullified to a substantial degree whatever benefit the mines would have had from that limited right to sell their product on the free market.

There was a good deal of criticism in regard to rigidity, and I think I was one of those who urged on the government that they should be much less rigid in the application of that policy, that they should remove some of the fetters that were still imposed upon the gold producers and let the producers enjoy as much benefit as they could from the still limited basis upon which they were entitled to enter the free market.
But let us come back to the point with which I was dealing. The minister conjures up the possibility that the United States might abandon its policy of purchasing newly mined gold at the price of $35 U. S. per ounce.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: I did not suggest that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958

The minister puts that before us and says that if the United States administration did so we would then be left holding a lot of gold and there would be criticism over our holding so much gold. If the Canadian government is going to hold itself aloof from all communication with the United States administration in this regard, then I suppose we are going to be operating in the dark. If the Canadian government would measure up to the responsibilities that I tried to describe earlier this afternoon it would not be very hard to learn what is United States policy in this regard or what are the possibilities of a departure from that policy.
I am sure there is no evidence that has come to the attention of any member of the government to suggest for one minute that the

United States administration is going to abandon or modify its policy of purchasing all newly mined gold offered at a fixed price of $35 U.S. per ounce. The modification we were urging that the Canadian government should seek was an upward adjustment in the price. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Villeneuve support this afternoon what we have been saying in that regard.
But it is all a question of what is good sense in relation to the total Canadian interest, and I think the Canadian government has an opportunity here to show its confidence in the future of this industry. It would have a good effect if the Canadian government, instead of contemplating a reduction in its holdings of gold as reserves, would say, "We have confidence in the future of this important Canadian commodity and we are going to increase rather than reduce our holdings of gold in our reserve fund".

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
I did not intend to suggest to the government for one minute that gold miners should be exempt from income tax or any other tax, because I know they want to pay their fair share. However, when the hon. member for Yukon was speaking yesterday with regard to a situation that exists in his particular constituency, his remarks gave me the thought of trading dollars. That was all. That is why I put that on the record. I should like to refer for a moment to our gold reserves. I am not going to say anything about the monetary fund because I do not know enough about it. I leave that to others who are much more capable than I am.
A few months ago a very responsible mining man made the statement at a public meeting that it looked as if the government was hoarding gold, not selling any to other countries but storing it, waiting for a higher price in order to profit from the production of the gold mines. I cannot speak for the government but I do not think any government would do anything like that. I have faith in gold. I think and hope that at some time in the near future it will come back and play its proper part in the Canadian economic sphere, and pay its own way. But I would suggest this. If the government does not export gold or sell any and if the price should go up, shall I say to $50 or $60 an ounce, the government would be making a considerable profit from the gold mines. If that should happen, consideration should be given to handing that profit back to those mines with a string attached, namely that a percentage of it would be given to the men who were employed in the mines at that time.
Secondary industry is one thing I wanted to mention. I spoke about it for a second and
Supply-National Revenue then I lost the trend of thought. As I said, I did not want to open up discussion of anything that was not relevant. However, there is one thing that is relevant to secondary industry, and that is the gas pipe line in northern Ontario, which is going to go right through my constituency. I believe this pipe line will have a big effect in attracting secondary industries into my constituency and into other constituencies in northern Ontario.
I do not want to put on the record any suggestion as to price, but it would appear to me that with a pipe line that is some 400 miles closer to the source of supply than, shall we say, cities like Toronto or Hamilton, we should enjoy a cheaper price for that fuel in my constituency. Time alone will tell whether or not we shall do so. If we enjoy a cheaper price, that fact will help us to compete, having regard to transportation problems, because we have to transport our products greater distances in order to reach a market.
That is about all I wish to say at this particular time. I hope those who are here when a similar bill comes before parliament in 1958-and I refer to members of all parties

will give it the good consideration that they have given it during the past seven years and will support it if the gold mines should need assistance.

In some years we have had them cut down as much as 10 per cent. It depends a good deal on the department. There are certain estimates put in covering undertakings that we decide should not be gone ahead with this year, and out it comes.

Then in freight and express there is an increase of $5,000; publication of regulations, memoranda and annual report, $5,000; repairs and upkeep of buildings and works, $25,000; light, power and water charges, $2,000. That is very easily explained. It is the result of the five-day week. We have to have a six days per week service in most places, and in some places seven days per week. In addition, there is the increase in the normal business of the country in imports and the like, and it takes more people and more officers; it takes more people because the ordinary people do five days' work and you have to provide for the extra days.
Does the minister's last statement mean that at most ordinary customs ports you can get things cleared on Saturday? That is not my impression.
No, but at border points it is sometimes very necessary to supply that service for more than the normal five days.

That is true of the ordinary border crossing points and relates to vehicular traffic, but the bulk of the ordinary customs clearance that is usually done at one of the ports of entry, that is where large shipments would have to be cleared, is not done on Saturday. If I am correct, I cannot follow why the five day week would impose the necessity for this large increase in staff.

It is not ordinarily done on Saturdays. There may be special circumstances, such as repair machinery or something like that which is imported, where an officer would have to go out and clear it. The vehicular traffic is much greater on the weekends than any other part of the week. Mr. Chairman, we will take note of that objection, look into the situation and try to improve it.

We have to provide for them because there is no other way of getting the money when you estimate in November of one year what you are going to need until a year from the next March. That is the way it is done; your fiscal year is the first of April to the end of March. You are estimating for about 18 months there. We base it on the average

growth over the years and the number of people we will need. That takes up quite a lot in salaries.
In addition to that you have to make provision in your estimates for an increase in salaried positions for the period of the next 18 months, so all told it cannot be estimated to the dollar and nobody expects that. We do attempt, however, to estimate as accurately as possible based upon our experience in former years.
Why would not the increase of $809,000 be added to what was actually spent in the last fiscal year rather than added to what you estimated for the last fiscal year?

Well, Mr. Chairman, that gives the actual expenditure and, as a matter of fact, that is good policy because we have saved money on what we received; yet we have to go ahead and provide for the normal increases there will be in position and wages. That is the principal item of all our expenses. If you go over them you will find this whole department is entirely administrative. I think 89 per cent of all the money we ask for is to pay in wages. Our next largest expenditure is to provide facilities in different parts of the country. Now, out in your part of the country we have spent money down at the Pacific highway. At Coutts, Alberta, it cost us about $1 million on account of changed conditions.
That is not under this vote.

No, but I am referring to former years and the changes that have taken place because of changed conditions. As the result of the development of the oil field in northern Alberta trucks by the thousands come over United States highways, enter Alberta at Coutts and go up to Lethbridge, Calgary and on to Edmonton. There are similar items at other places. Down at Lacolle in the province of Quebec we spent about $1 million for increased warehousing on account of the great traffic there from various states through Lacolle and Rouses Point and these other places leading into the city of Montreal. That obtains at Windsor, Fort Erie, Sarnia and at these places, Lacolle and Rouses Point; out in your country, at Coutts, Alberta and down the Pacific highway.
Last year I was down at the Pacific highway and I saw truckloads of cars going through there that had been exported by General Motors. They entered the United

States at Detroit, went clean across the country and came up north into British Columbia at the Pacific highway. We therefore have to have facilities to carry on that business, and it is increasing all the time.
That is all true and we are glad to see the development, but what I am criticizing is the method of estimating. Last year the department estimated it would require $23,806,542 or-
Where is that, on page 388?

Yes. The department spent
$650,000 less than that. In other words you overestimated last year by $650,000. You must have known that all these developments were taking place; they did not all happen overnight.
But take the other item right above that, "Less amount recoverable from firms requiring special services, $500,000." No one could tell whether that was going to be $5,000 or half a million.

But you estimated that you would need $24,306,542 and you only spent $23,153,000. This year you are estimating for $25,316,357, and I am just asking if it is not possible to get a little closer to the actual figures. It seems to me with a gap of $650,000 last year between what was voted and what was required the department may be quite a bit too high this year in the amount they are asking for. The Department of National Revenue of all departments should be able to estimate these figures accurately because this department has to raise the money.

Well, Mr. Chairman, it
appears to me I am being criticized for saving money.
No, you are being criticized for asking for more than you need.

Well, I know, but that is
only $800,000 out of $25 million, and that is about as close estimating as you can do.
But $800,000 is a lot of money.

Certainly it is, but what is it relative to? It is relative to the total expenditure we are asking here of $24,616,357, or $25 million without the receipts we take in. So I think that is as about as close estimating as I would ask the department to do. It works out better to have your estimates such that they will cover your expenditures than to have supplementary estimates or have to find some way of getting more money to carry on. There is a principle that is endorsed by the treasury board of changed allotments. We do not have the money in our department to switch it from one vote to another.

We find for example that last year a department asked for $1 million for an item and spent only $750,000; they come back this year and ask for $1,125,000. To the opposition it looks as though some sort of padding is going on. The net result is to budget for more money than is actually required. Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether this is the right item to bring up what I have in mind. They present figures to point out that the expectation in the United States is to have an increase of about 6 per cent this year in the production of turkeys as compared with last year, which may well result in a surplus of turkeys in the United States. May I suggest that this matter be brought up when the Minister of Finance is dealing with his items.
