289.	General administration, $2,702,629.

The estimates committee
dealt in some detail with the estimates of this department, and as a consequence I do not intend to ask too many questions concerning the individual items. However, I would like to point out that the law costs under item 389 have increased from $80,000 to $165,000, and under item 390 from $140,000 to $170,000, a total increase from $220,000 to $335,000. The increase amounts to $115,000 or over 50 per cent. When we queried the minister in committee we were told that there were one or two special cases. This is quite a sizeable increase and possibly the minister could give us some more details.
I understand that these law costs are involved in different places across the country where the department has instigated proceedings. I am wondering how the representatives of the legal fraternity are chosen, if there is a preferred list from which the lawyers are picked. It appears to me that the thinking of the Department of National Revenue, taxation division, has changed considerably in the last number of years. When a taxpayer or his representative went to the district office he received every courtesy, which is still the case, but there seems to be a change of thinking. Now it is, how much can we get?
The taxpayer should pay his just tax- there is no complaint about that at all-but when there is any give or take, as there is upon occasions, I am quite sure he does not very often get the benefit of it. I am not suggesting that the department should assist the taxpayer in making out his tax return. We appreciate that that is not right. He is supposed to be given assistance and advice and that sort of thing, but the various district officers of the taxation department work on directives to quite a degree, I would say, from the head office. They must come from the head office. These are supposed to be interpretations of the Income Tax Act and rulings by the department.
There has been a tendency, in recent times at least, no doubt as the result of directives to the various district offices, as to how to interpret capital gains. As a result, in some instances we almost have the capital gains tax despite what the various ministers of

finance have said over the past few years to the effect that we do not have one and they are not in favour of it. When inquiry of the minister was made on this matter he maintained that all the departmental officials did was to follow the letter of the act.
In questioning the minister we came to the conclusion that possibly he would be in a position to offer advice to the Minister of Finance as to changing some of the provisions of the Income Tax Act. Several times we suggested to him that he take up this matter with the Minister of Finance. There were several instances in the evidence where he admitted there were inequities as regards the collection of taxes and perhaps as regards the actual rulings or the interpretations placed on them. If they need clarification, I think the Minister of National Revenue should advise the Minister of Finance that these items should be clarified.
If the departmental officials' rulings did not result in costing the taxpayers money, possibly nobody would complain, but I contend that some of the money that the taxpayer has to pay in his own defence is unnecessary. In an appeal board case the taxpayer puts up his $15. If he wins his appeal he is refunded his $15. In the meantime he has perhaps had legal and accounting advice costing him, we may say, hundreds of dollars, and I am given to understand he is not permitted to deduct those expenses in future years. The minister might correct me if I am wrong in that, but I think that evidence was given.
I had the feeling in the committee as we went through these various items and through the discussion periods that although many times we contended that the Department of National Revenue should advise the Department of Finance on certain corrections in the interpretation or in the actual wording of the act so the interpretations would be more just and equitable, there was a reluctance on the part of the department to so advise. In fact I almost felt as though it did not want them to be corrected. There seems to be an atmosphere-as a matter of fact it is the case-in the department that the taxpayer is actually guilty until he proves himself innocent. This is far from what we have always considered as ordinary British justice, in that it has always been felt that any person is innocent until proven guilty.
We mentioned in the committee a few instances of what we felt were inequities. We suggested to the minister that he bring these to the attention of the Minister of Finance. As one small item, I am given to understand that an actor who is working on salary and is on tour cannot deduct the expenses of his tour.
Supply-National Revenue The minister was intimating that he was allowed his expenses, that he got an increased salary because of the simple fact that he was not allowed to make deductions. However, he is paying tax on that increased amount. In other words he has to pay tax on what would be considered additional increment for travelling expenses.
There was another point that we brought to the attention of the minister, and it seems to be a question of a ruling. The departmental officials admitted that a party willing a farm to his son is allowed at present a fair market value, whereas if a farmer sells to his son the son cannot deduct depreciation of an amount greater than the residual value, one might say, in the father's hands. There is no doubt that this is penalizing the son. I understand that the minister has intimated that some adjustment has been or is being recommended to the Department of Finance, but the whole thing is so ridiculous that I think it is high time something was actually done.
I should like to say a few words on the iniquitous net worth system of collecting taxes, and it applies to all people, not only to farmers. First of all I should like to mention to the minister that I quite realize that he and his departmental officials have a very tough job and a very unenviable one. After all, collecting taxes is coming close to a man's pocket, and he does not like it. I realize that they meet circumstances which the average person in business possibly does not meet, because the taxpayer sometimes feels he does not get full value for his tax. However, I am not concerned, in speaking of net worth, with the treatment of a case after it has actually got into the chief assessor's hands in an income tax district office. As I say, one gets very courteous treatment from the officials. I realize that they will listen to reason when it can be shown where a previous statement made was not correct or had been misunderstood by an inspector who had made the original assessment, and that sort of thing is very frequently adjusted.
I am not so much concerned with the taxpayer who has had legal or accounting advice from the beginning of the case. If he has been advised by his lawyer or his accountant, then I think it is up to the lawyer or accountant to shoulder any responsibility. I am not concerned about that taxpayer, but I am concerned about the individual taxpayer who has not filed a return. Perhaps he should have filed the tax return, and perhaps he has never filed one. Very frequently many of them are not actually taxable. However, the taxation department inspector or some official in the district office who keeps files on all

Supply-National Revenue sorts of things, thinks that a certain resident of a community should be paying taxes. He probably gets a demand for a tax return for one, two or three years, and he files it. He is a farmer and he is entitled to file on the cash system. He does not appear to have to pay any tax on that basis. The cash system shows that he should not pay any tax. However, the department may have some further reason for thinking he should, so an inspector goes to visit the man. The inspector, failing sufficient documents and records covering the past few years, undoubtedly will undertake to make up a net worth statement. He asks questions as to the date of purchase of equipment, the farm and that sort of thing.
One of the purposes of the questions is to prepare a depreciation schedule so the farmer can actually be allowed proper depreciation when the time comes to prepare his net worth statement. However, I do not think sufficient questions are asked as to what possible disposals the farmer may have made of machinery or equipment, which disposals are capital gains and not taxable.
Then we come to living expenses. I do not know of any particular case myself but I have heard some pretty gruesome tales of things that have happened such as the inspector making a tour of the house and all that sort of thing without the owner's consent. But X do know that many personal questions are asked as to what the man has spent.
In this connection we have to remember that the inspector is dealing with somebody who has not had any previous experience with this sort of thing and no doubt he is frightened stiff because the inspector is there. First of all he should be put at his ease and should have things explained to him by the inspector. When the inspector is asking him what money he may have spent personally I think he should point out to the man the simple fact that the more he claims to have spent the more it is going to cost him taxwise. The average person does not understand that and I think that is a simple courtesy that should be extended. I do not believe it is done. From the evidence we receive I understand it is not.
A summary of the various living expenses is detailed, and let us not forget that it is probably all done very hurriedly. The inspector has not spent two, three or four days there. I imagine he has spent a morning, and then moves on to some other place in the afternoon. But the inspector may have covered a period of six years. He has asked these questions, has got a list of so-called living expenses, and the farmer is asked to sign it.

I am quite free to admit that I have known instances where, after the farmer has signed one of these statements as to his living expenses, the amount has been changed. If he can prove that he was wrong in his guess as to a certain item, that a certain medical bill was paid or something like that, that is quite all right. The department will change the amount. But at the same time there is no doubt that once the farmer has signed the statement there is something there that is used upon occasion.
I admit, as I say, that I have known cases where the assessment has been prepared and then changed after somebody has been able to prove something to the satisfaction of the department, but I have also known cases where the assessor has intimated to the taxpayer that he may have something there but if he changes it the department will change his living expenses so the amount of tax may well remain the same as in the initial assessment. To me that is absolutely wrong, and I think it should be stopped. I am not saying anything against these inspectors as individuals other than I do not think they know what they are dealing with. I do not think they know the problems of the farmer. I doubt if very many of them have ever lived on a farm. I do not think they realize how a farmer lives. He does not live as a city man does. He does not spend money on personal living expenses. He does not wear the same kind of clothes, because he does not have to in his particular occupation.
I believe these inspectors should have a better knowledge of the industry with which they are dealing when they set out to make up one of these net worth statements. My contention is that the average farmer, unless he is specializing in some particular cash crop or in poultry, beef cattle, fur farming, or something of that nature, does not do any more over his lifetime than pay off his mortgage. As a consequence I think there are a great number of farmers throughout the country who are being victimized, one might almost say. I believe that the average farmer, the average citizen, wishes to pay his tax just as much as any inspector might wish him to, and he wants to pay his just tax. Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest that the department should readjust its thinking to a point where it will not believe that every taxpayer is guilty of evasion.

Mr. Chairman, before this item passes I should like to appeal to the minister to clarify the government's position on capital gains. As he knows, this matter came before the estimates committee but I for one felt that the explanation still was not

clear enough. Hon. members know that in Canada we have never officially had a capital gains tax. We have not had such a tax because it has been felt that in a new, developing country every encouragement should be given to venture capital, and I think that is a sound attitude. If we had a capital gains tax today risk capital would probably be discouraged.
Several months ago the Minister of Finance made a public statement to the effect that the government's attitude toward a capital gains tax had not recently changed, but I cannot help wondering whether the officials of the department we are now discussing read that statement or are aware of it, because fears have been expressed recently in many quarters that without any new authority from parliament the department has been pursuing a policy which could alter completely the concept of taxable income in Canada. Recently, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Perth, there have been examples of the Department of National Revenue taxing gains or profits made on real estate transactions, and there have been examples where the department has taxed profits made in the stock market. I think there have been examples where the department has taxed profits made in the buying and selling of mortgages.
I think most Canadians and most members of parliament have considered up to now that this kind of profit was a legitimate capital gain, and they cannot understand why such gains should be taxed. The income tax laws in the past, unwisely I think, have given a good deal of leeway to the departmental officials to decide what is capital gain and what is income. Until recently I think the departmental officials have been fairly liberal in interpreting the law, but in the past few years they seem to be getting a little bit stiffer in their attitude, and I believe there is a very real fear in the country today that Canada may be getting a capital gains tax not by any act of parliament but through the interpretation given to the law by the taxation officials.
There are certain judicial decisions which have tended to increase those fears. Because our laws at the present time do not define capital gain and do not define income, the Canadian courts appear to have been extending the concept of business transactions subject to income tax.
Mr. Chairman, what I want to say is this. If we are to have a capital gains tax, then let parliament pass the law bringing it in. I do not think it should be brought in by any back-door method. I would call on the government this afternoon to give a clear-cut definition-by statute if necessary-as to what
Supply-National Revenue is capital gain and what is income. Then the people of Canada would know where they could go from there. In other words, I think the government should spell out precisely what are the definitions of these terms. I would appreciate it if either the Minister of National Revenue or the Minister of Finance would comment on that matter, and I wish they would do it this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to express my agreement with what the hon. member for Perth had to say about the net worth statement, particularly as it referred to farmers. It has been my experience as well as his-and perhaps it has been that of others who have had something to do with assisting farmers in making their returns -that in many cases the farmers have been victimized by a lack of knowledge on the one hand of what is required and on the other hand by officials who were a bit too arbitrary in setting down in the net worth statement their own interpretation of the values on the farm.
There are two chief ways in which, in my opinion, the assessments are made higher than they should be in regard to net worth statements, namely the overvaluation of the buildings and equipment which are found on the farm at the end of a particular period, and the undervaluation of the equipment and, in some cases, buildings that were disposed of during the period in question. There is also the question of the cost of living. I think that is a real injustice which would warrant a fairly close look by the department, where inspectors take it upon themselves to decide what the farmer's cost of living is over the years.
I have examined personally a good many net worth statements in the last five or six years, and I can say that in almost every case they have materially overestimated the real cost of living of the average farmer. There are exceptional cases, of course, always. There may be some farmers who are in the habit through necessity, of spending a great deal more money than others; but on the average I have found the tendency to be to overestimate the farmer's cost of living. The difficulty arises here because no farmer-nor, I suspect, is any other person-in our country is in a position to go back five or six years and prove to the inspector or to the department what his actual personal expenditures were. People have become more or less conscious of the necessity of keeping records of their business transactions, whether it is on the farm or elsewhere, because they realize that is part and parcel of their income tax return. But no one has been in the habit of keeping a very close track of his personal

Supply-National Revenue expenditures. And when it comes to the point of the farmer's word against the word of the inspector, the department naturally will accept the word of their own officials. I think some real injustices have resulted with regard to these net worth statements on account of the factors I have mentioned, as was very well set out by the hon. member for Perth.
However, there is another angle with regard to this item that I wish to pursue at this time. It arises out of a question asked in this house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on April 9 of this year. The question will be found at page 2729 of Hansard. I shall read the question and the answer in order to set out the background clearly. On that occasion the hon. member asked a question of the Minister of National Revenue in these words:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Will the minister re-examine the income tax files of the breweries of Manitoba to ascertain whether any of them claimed income tax deductibility for the contributions they made, as revealed in Winnipeg last week, to the Liberal, Conservative and Social Credit parties of Manitoba?
At that time the minister replied as follows:
1 can comply with the request of the hon. gentleman but I doubt very much whether I can give him information about other people's business.
Then as a supplementary question the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked:
May I make it clear that I did not ask the minister to give publicity to information that is secret by law. I asked him if he would examine the files to ascertain for the benefit of the treasury whether or not such deductibility was claimed by the breweries of Manitoba. May I assume the minister will conduct such an examination?
The minister's reply was this:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the question and will take it into consideration.
No doubt the question is still under consideration and will be under consideration for some time to come. At this time I think it would be only fair to the minister and to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to set out the background upon which his question was based. I think it is also necessary to point out certain things to the committee and to the minister because of the fact that ministers do not seem to be aware of the basis upon which these questions were asked. I find that on the same day I directed to the Minister of Justice a question in the following terms:
Mr.^ Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Justice. Is the minister aware of any financial contributions made by the breweries to the party with which he is associated?
The reply I received was:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is no.

It was to me a rather astounding answer, because for a week or ten days prior to that time, we had been reading newspaper headlines and hearing over the radio about the rather astounding developments in Manitoba with regard to these contributions. Yet one of the ministers of the crown gives the answer that he was not aware of it.
In case the minister may think this has to do only with the situation in the province of Manitoba, may I refer to the statement made by the representative of the breweries in giving evidence before the committee of the Manitoba legislature on April 6, 1956. I shall not read it all. If the minister wishes me to do so I will send it across to him. In that statement you will find that the representative of the breweries stated that not only did the breweries of Manitoba make cash contributions to the political parties within the province of Manitoba but that they made them also to the federal political parties. That immediately, of course, involves the consideration of this parliament.
I think it is a perfectly fair question to ask whether the minister and his department have in fact carefully and scrupulously checked the income tax returns of these breweries-and the same, of course, applies to any other corporation which makes financial contributions to political parties-in order to make sure that they did not do this at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. I personally suspect very much that not only are the breweries of this country and some of the other corporations using undue influence upon the political parties in this country, but that they are doing so at the expense of the public treasury. I believe that, in fact, they are claiming deductibility from income with respect to their income tax for moneys spent either in cash or perhaps to a greater extent in some of the huge advertising campaigns they put on in order to assist the political party of their choice, which expenditure is marked down as advertising from a business point of view but which is not really advertising at all but is propaganda in the pure sense of the word.
In case the minister or the committee is in doubt about what happened in Manitoba, may I refer them to some of the newspaper headlines. For example, the Winnipeg Free Press of April 4,	1956, carried this headline,
"Breweries Bare Gifts to Three Parties; All But C.C.F. Shared $28,075 since 1945". May I point out that this $28,000 was raised to about $30,000 later, and that refers only to contributions made to political parties within the province of Manitoba. The figures with respect to contributions made in the larger field to the federal parties were not revealed,

because the evidence was given before a committee which had to do with liquor profits in the province of Manitoba.
May I just comment that the thing that struck me when I read this headline was the reference to "gifts" to the three political parties. I think that was a rather unfortunate use of the word "gifts", because I do not consider these moneys as gifts at all, and I am sure the political parties concerned did not either. They could be more correctly described as cash advances to the political parties concerned, and particularly the Liberal party because the next headline is in the following terms:	"Liberals Got Lion's Share
of Donations". It was revealed to the committee that they got 59 per cent or $16,400 of the total.
These financial contributions to political parties are made for a purpose. None of us is so naive as to think for a moment that this is done out of the goodness of heart of the breweries or any other corporations because they have so much money they do not know what to do with it, and so they decide to give some of it to the political parties. The fact that none of it was asked for or given to the C.C.F. indicates it is being done for the purpose of promoting the political parties of their choice. Incidentally, I mentioned the two major political parties, the Liberals and the Conservatives, but there was a small amount for the Social Credit party, about $500. Considering that they have not been in power in Manitoba or Ottawa, I suppose you could put that down as unearned income.
I would say this, that the breweries involved broke no law when they made financial contributions to the political parties of their choice. They are permitted to do so under the elections act, provided there is no evidence to show that they either asked for or were promised any economic considerations for the moneys they turned over to these parties. But there is a moral side to it. There is a moral law which is even more important, and that is to what extent are these breweries, such as the ones in Manitoba which deal directly with the government and were instrumental in influencing the government to set a price for beer which resulted in four breweries making a profit of over $18 million-

This has nothing to do with a discussion of the administration of the taxation division. I can make a statement in 10 words that will clear up this point. It is to the effect that political contributions are not a deductible expense of doing business for any organization in this country.

The statement may be in 10 words or it may take 10 hours, but so far as I 67509-318
Supply-National Revenue am concerned that is not the question. The point I am getting at is that these breweries are making these contributions to the political parties of this country, and in my opinion there is a danger that they are padding their expenses with regard to income in order to hide that money which is going out in the form of contributions.
The minister says it is not deductible. We have attempted on several occasions to find out from the minister whether any attempt has been made, without asking for the names of the corporations or the breweries concerned, by these corporations to claim deductibility. The minister has refused to answer. Apparently on April 9 the minister was not as sure as he claims to be today, because then he said he would take the matter under consideration. If he were going to take it under consideration on April 9 of this year, it would indicate he had not given it any consideration before that time. I think that statement by the Minister of National Revenue on April 9 was an admission that the department and the minister had not given proper consideration to that situation, but had in fact neglected the public treasury by leaving the door open to these breweries to make political contributions to these three political parties, for the purpose of influencing these parties.
Now, I hope that in the future what the minister has just stated will be strictly adhered to and carried out. I hope the minister can assure the house that no corporation, or any other business for that matter, will have the privilege of using their income for the purpose of making cash contributions or paying for huge advertisements which are, in fact, propaganda and not business advertisements, and then deducting that amount from their income in order to reduce their taxable assessment and reduce the amount of taxes which should go to the public treasury.
I want to make it quite clear that I do not think it is moral or right that the huge corporations of this country should make large amounts of money available to the political parties. I do not think it is a good thing for democracy that the political parties of this country should be influenced by the huge monopolies in this country. At the same time, it is adding insult to injury when you realize it is possible for those corporations to do that and deduct the amount from their income and thus make the public treasury pay for the propaganda which they are putting out in favour of the parties of their choice.
